claims.text: Takeaway 2 / protects section: people with private insurance are protected for most emergency services, non-emergency services from out-of-network providers at in-network facilities, and out-of-network air ambulance
claims.quote: The No Surprises Act protects people covered under group and individual health plans from receiving surprise medical bills when they receive most emergency services, non-emergency services from out-of-network providers at in-network facilities, and services from out-of-network air ambulance service providers.

claims.text: Takeaway 3 / protects section / FAQ 'Do I have to pay': you can't be charged more than in-network cost-sharing
claims.quote: Ban out-of-network cost-sharing (like out-of-network coinsurance or copayments) for most emergency and some non-emergency services. You can't be charged more than in-network cost-sharing for these services.

claims.text: Protects list item 1 / FAQ emergency room: most emergency services even out of network and without prior authorization
claims.quote: Ban surprise bills for most emergency services, even if you get them out-of-network and without approval beforehand (prior authorization).

claims.text: Protects list item 2 / FAQ balance billing: certain services like anesthesiology or radiology from out-of-network providers during a visit to an in-network facility
claims.quote: Ban out-of-network charges and balance bills for certain additional services (like anesthesiology or radiology) furnished by out-of-network providers as part of a patient's visit to an in-network facility.

claims.text: Citable summary / FAQ 'What is a surprise medical bill': CMS term for an unexpected balance bill from an out-of-network provider; difference between billed charge and what the plan paid
claims.quote: could bill you for the difference between the billed charge and the amount your health plan paid ... An unexpected balance bill from an out-of-network provider is also called a surprise medical bill.

claims.text: Citable summary: starting in 2022, bans the most common types for people with private insurance; uninsured/self-pay can often get a good faith estimate up front
claims.quote: Starting in 2022 ... If you have private health insurance, these new protections ban the most common types of surprise bills. If you're uninsured ... you can often get a good faith estimate

claims.quote: If you get health coverage through your employer, a Health Insurance Marketplace®, [1] or an individual health insurance plan you purchase directly from an insurance company, these new rules will:

claims.text: Definition of surprise billing
claims.quote: Surprise billing occurs when you have health coverage and unknowingly or unavoidably receive care from an out-of-network provider or at an out-of-network healthcare facility and are billed directly for that care when your health plan does not cover

claims.text: Definition of balance billing (difference between billed charge and allowed amount)
claims.quote: the out-of-network provider or healthcare facility could bill you directly for the difference between their billed charge and the amount your health plan will to pay for the charge (the "allowed amount"). This is called "balance billing."

claims.text: Examples: out-of-network anesthesiologist after surgery at an in-network facility, emergency room, air ambulance
claims.quote: Visited the emergency room for treatment, only to receive a surprise bill? Had major surgery performed at an in-network facility ... only to receive an unexpected bill from an out-of-network anesthesiologist? ... air ambulance ride

claims.text: Cost-sharing counts toward in-network deductible and out-of-pocket maximum
claims.quote: Any cost-sharing payments you make must count toward your in-network deductible or out-of-pocket maximums as if an in-network provider charged them.

claims.text: If plan does not cover air ambulance at all (or a ground ambulance transports you), you may be responsible for the uncovered amount
claims.quote: However, if your plan does not cover air ambulance services at all or if a ground ambulance transports you, then you may be responsible for the uncovered amount.

claims.text: Not every unexpected bill is covered; can still be billed for services not covered by the plan
claims.quote: It does not cover every unexpected or high medical bill. For example, you can still be billed for services and treatments that are not covered by your plan.

claims.text: Notice and consent not permitted for emergency services before stabilization or for ancillary services (emergency medicine, anesthesiology, pathology, radiology, neonatology); FAQ waive
claims.quote: In emergency situations, notice and consent is not permitted when providing: any emergency services before your condition is stabilized ... notice and consent is not permitted for ancillary services ... related to emergency medicine, anesthesiology, pathology, radiology, and neonatology

claims.text: FAQ waive: notice and consent may be used for some scheduled non-emergency services or post-stabilization care; signing is your choice
claims.quote: you schedule certain non-emergency services (other than ancillary services) at an in-network healthcare facility, or you need post-stabilization care after an emergency ... Signing this form is entirely your choice.

claims.text: EOB shows what the plan will pay and what you owe
claims.quote: The EOB tells you what services you got, when you got them, how much your plan will pay, and how much you owe.

claims.text: Contact the No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059 if bill exceeds EOB cost sharing or the law is not followed
claims.quote: Contact the No Surprises Help Desk at (1 800) 985-3059 if: you receive a bill that exceeds what the EOB shows you owe in cost sharing ... you believe that the No Surprises Act is not being followed

claims.text: Takeaway 5 / no-insurance section / FAQ good faith estimate: usually must give a good faith estimate on request or when scheduled at least 3 business days ahead
claims.quote: Usually, if you aren't using health insurance to pay for your care, your health care provider must give you a good faith estimate of expected charges if you request one or schedule services at least 3 business days in advance.

claims.text: Estimate covers a single provider or facility; e.g. separate estimates from surgeon and hospital
claims.quote: Good faith estimates only list expected charges for a single provider or facility. ... You should request 2 good faith estimates: one from the surgeon, and one from the hospital.

references.record_title: Know your medical bill rights when using insurance | CMS

claims.text: Non-emergency protections apply to care related to a visit to an in-network hospital, hospital outpatient department or ambulatory surgical center; air ambulance
claims.quote: The Act protects you from unexpected out-of-network bills from: Emergency room visits; Non-emergency care related to a visit to an in-network: Hospital; Hospital outpatient department; Ambulatory surgical center; Air ambulance services

claims.text: Applies to employer, Marketplace and individual market coverage
claims.quote: These protections apply to you if you have health insurance through an employer (including a Federal Employees Health Benefits plan), the federal Health Insurance Marketplace, a State-based Marketplace, or other individual market coverage.

claims.text: Emergency room includes hospital ERs and independent freestanding emergency departments; post-stabilization protected in most cases
claims.quote: Emergency rooms at a hospital; Independent, freestanding emergency departments ... After an emergency room visit, you're protected from unexpected out-of-network bills for post-stabilization services in most cases.

claims.text: Example: in-network hospital with out-of-network attending physician
claims.quote: For example, your local hospital may be in-network, but an attending physician might be out-of-network.

claims.text: Some health plans don't cover emergency care
claims.quote: Note: Some health plans don't cover emergency care.

claims.text: Ground ambulance can still charge out-of-network rates and cost-sharing unless state law bars it; FAQ ground ambulance state law
claims.quote: Currently, ground ambulance services aren't covered by billing protections in the No Surprises Act. They're still allowed to charge out-of-network rates and cost-sharing (unless they're not allowed to under state law).

claims.text: Planned-care protections don't apply in other settings like a doctor's office or at an out-of-network facility
claims.quote: These protections don't apply at other settings (like a doctor's office that isn't a hospital outpatient department), or if you go to an out-of-network facility.

claims.text: Exceptions: short-term limited duration, health care sharing ministry, fixed indemnity plans; vision-only and dental-only generally
claims.quote: These balance billing protections generally don't apply to vision-only and dental-only insurance plans ... Short-term limited duration and health care sharing ministry plans ... Fixed indemnity excepted benefits plans, like hospital indemnity insurance

claims.text: Medicare, Medicaid, IHS, VA, TRICARE already protect from some unexpected out-of-network bills
claims.quote: Do you use Medicare, Medicaid, Indian Health Services, Veterans Affairs Health Care, or TRICARE? These plans already protect you from some unexpected out-of-network bills.

claims.text: Notice and consent for some out-of-network care at an in-network facility or post-stabilization; signing is your choice; you will likely pay more; FAQ balance billing (signing gives up protections)
claims.quote: Signing this form means that you agree to get care out-of-network and give up your protections from unexpected out-of-network bills. ... You will likely have to pay more ... Signing the notice and consent form is your choice.

claims.text: No good faith estimate during emergency care
claims.quote: Note: You won't get an estimate during emergency care.

claims.text: Dispute within 120 days of getting the initial bill
claims.quote: You have to start a dispute within 120 days (about 4 months) of getting your initial bill.

claims.text: $400 threshold is per provider or facility against that provider's or facility's own good faith estimate
claims.quote: with respect to the total billed charges by a provider or facility, an amount that is at least $400 more than the total amount of expected charges listed on the good faith estimate for the provider or facility.

claims.text: Deadline: 120 calendar days of receiving the initial bill
claims.quote: postmarked within 120 calendar days of receiving the initial bill containing charges for the item or service that is substantially in excess of the expected charges in the good faith estimate.

claims.text: Good faith estimate on request or when scheduled at least 3 business days ahead
claims.quote: When a primary item or service is scheduled at least 3 business days before the date the item or service is scheduled to be furnished: Not later than 1 business day after the date of scheduling

claims.text: Good faith estimate when requested by the uninsured or self-pay individual
claims.quote: When a good faith estimate is requested by an uninsured (or self-pay) individual: Not later than 3 business days after the date of the request.

claims.text: $25 non-refundable administrative fee to file a dispute
claims.quote: You'll need to pay a $25 non-refundable administrative fee to file a dispute.

claims.text: If insurer decided not to pay and you think it violates the Act, appeal following plan documents and denial notices
claims.quote: Your insurer may have decided not to pay part or all of a claim. If you think this decision violates the No Surprises Act, appeal your bill. Follow the process described in your plan's documents and denial notices.
